theory.intro: To find a probability for a sample mean, standardise with $z=\dfrac{\bar{x}-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}$. The divisor is the standard deviation of $\bar{X}$, not of one observation, so a sample mean sits much closer to $\mu$ than a single value does.
facts: By the central limit theorem $\bar{X}$ is approximately $N\left(\mu,\dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}\right)$ when the sample is random and $n\ge 30$.

Standardise a **single observation** with $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$, using $\sigma$ and no $\sqrt{n}$. This measures its standardised distance from the mean. Normal-table probabilities and normal-tail comparisons for individual observations require a normally distributed population; the central limit theorem applies to sample means.
Read the stem carefully: one observation and a sample mean give different $z$ values from the same number.
Under the approximate normal sampling model, $P(\bar{X}>\mu)\approx0.5$, because the normal model is symmetrical about $\mu$.
Because $\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$ is small, a sample mean only a little away from $\mu$ can be very unlikely.
Shade the required region on the curve of $\bar{X}$ first, because the probability is the area of the shaded part.
steps: Write the mean and the standard deviation $\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$ of $\bar{X}$
Shade the region on the curve and find its area

workedExamples.question_text: A population has mean $150$ and standard deviation $24$. An independent random sample of $64$ values has mean $154.5$. Find the $z$-score of this sample mean.
workedExamples.solution_text:
The standard deviation of the sample mean is
$\begin{align*}\sigma_{\bar{X}}&=\frac{24}{\sqrt{64}}\\&=3.\end{align*}$
Standardise using this spread:
$\begin{align*}z&=\frac{154.5-150}{3}\\&=1.5.\end{align*}$

workedExamples.question_text: A population has mean $200$ g and standard deviation $30$ g. An independent random sample of $100$ items is taken. Using the empirical rule, estimate (a) $P(\bar{X}>206)$ and (b) $P(\bar{X}>197)$.
A population has mean $80$ and standard deviation $18$. An independent random sample of $81$ values is taken. Using the empirical rule, estimate (a) $P(76<\bar{X}<84)$ and (b) $P(78<\bar{X}<84)$.

A population has mean $110$ and standard deviation $25$. An independent random sample of $100$ values is taken. Estimate (a) $P(\bar{X}>113)$ and (b) $P(\bar{X}<108)$ using the table.
$\begin{array}{c|c}z&P(Z<z)\\\hline0.80&0.7881\\1.20&0.8849\end{array}$
workedExamples.solution_text:
The sampling distribution is approximately normal, with
$\begin{align*}\sigma_{\bar{X}}&=\frac{25}{\sqrt{100}}\\&=2.5.\end{align*}$
(a)
$\begin{align*}z&=\frac{113-110}{2.5}\\&=1.2.\\P(\bar{X}>113)&\approx P(Z>1.2)\\&=1-0.8849\\&=0.1151.\end{align*}$
(b) Use symmetry for the negative boundary:
$\begin{align*}z&=\frac{108-110}{2.5}\\&=-0.8.\\P(\bar{X}<108)&\approx P(Z<-0.8)\\&=1-P(Z<0.8)\\&=1-0.7881\\&=0.2119.\end{align*}$

workedExamples.question_text:
Individual package masses are normally distributed with mean $400$ g and standard deviation $20$ g. Compare a single package with the mean of an independent random sample of $64$ packages. Find the $z$-score of $405$ g in each case and the probability of exceeding $405$ g, using the table.
$\begin{array}{c|c}z&P(Z<z)\\\hline0.25&0.5987\\2.00&0.9772\end{array}$
workedExamples.solution_text:
For a single package, use the population standard deviation:
$\begin{align*}z_X&=\frac{405-400}{20}\\&=0.25.\\P(X>405)&=1-0.5987\\&=0.4013.\end{align*}$
For the sample mean, use
$\begin{align*}\sigma_{\bar{X}}&=\frac{20}{\sqrt{64}}\\&=2.5\text{ g}.\\z_{\bar{X}}&=\frac{405-400}{2.5}\\&=2.\\P(\bar{X}>405)&=1-0.9772\\&=0.0228.\end{align*}$
Both distributions are normal because the population is normal. The sample mean has the smaller spread and the larger $z$-score, so its right-tail probability is smaller.

workedExamples.question_text: A population has mean $90$ and standard deviation $40$. Independent random samples of $100$ values are taken. Using the empirical rule, estimate (a) the boundary $c$ for which $P(\bar{X}>c)\approx0.16$, (b) the interval symmetric about $90$ containing the middle $95\%$ of sample means, and (c) the width of the interval containing the middle $68\%$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
The sampling distribution is approximately normal, with
$\begin{align*}\sigma_{\bar{X}}&=\frac{40}{\sqrt{100}}\\&=4.\end{align*}$
(a) A right-tail area of approximately $0.16$ corresponds to $z=1$.
$\begin{align*}c&=90+1(4)\\&=94.\end{align*}$
(b) The middle $95\%$ corresponds approximately to $-2<Z<2$.
$\begin{align*}\text{Lower boundary}&=90-2(4)=82,\\\text{Upper boundary}&=90+2(4)=98.\end{align*}$
The interval is approximately $82<\bar{X}<98$.
(c) The middle $68\%$ corresponds approximately to $-1<Z<1$, giving boundaries $86$ and $94$.
$\begin{align*}\text{Width}&=94-86\\&=8.\end{align*}$

workedExamples.question_text: A population has mean $100$ and standard deviation $27$. Find the size of an independent random sample for which the standard deviation of the sample mean is $3$. Then use the empirical rule to estimate $P(\bar{X}>106)$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Solve for the sample size:
$\begin{align*}\frac{27}{\sqrt{n}}&=3,\\\sqrt{n}&=9,\\n&=81.\end{align*}$
Since $n=81\ge30$, use the approximately normal sampling distribution.
$\begin{align*}z&=\frac{106-100}{3}\\&=2.\\P(\bar{X}>106)&\approx P(Z>2)\\&\approx\frac{1-0.95}{2}\\&=0.025.\end{align*}$

foundation.question_text:
A population has mean $500$ g and standard deviation $60$ g. A random sample of $36$ items is taken.
Find the probability that the **sample mean** exceeds $520$ g, using the empirical rule.

A population has mean $180$ and standard deviation $28$.
A random sample of $49$ values is taken.
Find the probability that the **sample mean** lies between $172$ and $188$, using the empirical rule.

A population has mean $64$ and standard deviation $35$.
A random sample of $49$ values is taken.
Find the probability that the **sample mean** lies between $59$ and $74$, using the empirical rule.

A population has mean $120$ and standard deviation $18$.
A random sample of $81$ values gives a sample mean of $123$.
Find the $z$-score of this sample mean.

A population has mean $60$ and standard deviation $12$.
Find the $z$-score of the value $66$ when it is a single observation, and the $z$-score of $66$ when it is the mean of a random sample of $36$ values.
foundation.solution_text:
For a single observation the divisor is $\sigma$.
$z=\dfrac{66-60}{12}$
$=0.5$
For a sample mean the divisor is $\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}=\dfrac{12}{\sqrt{36}}=2$.
$z=\dfrac{66-60}{2}$
$=3$

A population has mean $500$ and standard deviation $40$.
A random sample of $100$ values is taken.
Find the probability that the **sample mean** lies between $496$ and $504$, using the empirical rule.

A population has mean $25$ and standard deviation $6$.
A random sample of $144$ values gives a sample mean of $26.2$.

A normally distributed population has mean $800$ and standard deviation $50$.
State which is smaller, the probability that a single observation exceeds $810$ or the probability that the mean of a random sample of $100$ observations exceeds $810$.
Support your answer with the two $z$-scores.
development.solution_text:
For a single observation the divisor is $\sigma=50$.
$z=\dfrac{810-800}{50}$
$=0.2$
For the sample mean the divisor is $\dfrac{50}{\sqrt{100}}=5$.
$z=\dfrac{810-800}{5}$
$=2$
A larger $z$ leaves a smaller right tail, so the probability for the sample mean is smaller.

mastery.question_text:
A population has mean $70$ and standard deviation $16$.
Find the sample size $n$ for which the standard deviation of $\bar{X}$ is $2$, and then use the empirical rule to find $P(\bar{X}>74)$ for that sample size.

A population has mean $250$ and standard deviation $36$.
Random samples of size $81$ are taken.
Find the interval, symmetrical about the mean, inside which $95\%$ of the sample means lie.
mastery.solution_text:
$\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}=\dfrac{36}{\sqrt{81}}$
$=4$
The central $95\%$ runs from $z=-2$ to $z=2$.
$250-2\times 4=242$
$250+2\times 4=258$
$95\%$ of sample means lie between $242$ and $258$.

mastery.question_text:
Individual readings of the flow rate of juice poured by a machine are normally distributed with mean $6.4$ mL per second and standard deviation $1.2$ mL per second.
Find the probability that a single flow-rate reading exceeds $6.8$ mL per second, and the probability that the mean of a random sample of $36$ flow-rate readings exceeds $6.8$ mL per second.
Round each $z$-score to two decimal places and use this table.
$\begin{array}{c|c} z & P(Z<z) \\ \hline 0.33 & 0.6293 \\ 0.67 & 0.7486 \\ 1.00 & 0.8413 \\ 2.00 & 0.9772 \end{array}$
mastery.solution_text:
For a single reading the divisor is $\sigma=1.2$.
$z=\dfrac{6.8-6.4}{1.2}$
$=0.33$
$P(X>6.8)=1-0.6293$
$=0.3707$
For the sample mean the divisor is $\dfrac{1.2}{\sqrt{36}}=0.2$.
$z=\dfrac{6.8-6.4}{0.2}$
$=2$
$P(\bar{X}>6.8)=1-0.9772$
$=0.0228$
